Crows recognising faces is a well-documented, counterintuitive claim from the University of Washington mask studies, and it fits the direct-claim hooks that gave our best skip rates. For the DIRECT OPEN test, slide 1's title is the strongest sentence on its own. Its body gives the key proof in 15 words with no highlight. There are 4 content slides with short text. This Reel also runs the follow-conversion experiment: the CTA promises Part 2, which will be crow intelligence (tools, counting, funerals) posted tomorrow. topic: Crows recognize human faces and hold grudges (UW mask study)
hook: Crows remember your face for years

slides.title: Crows remember your face for years
slides.body: In Seattle, scientists in masks trapped crows. Years later, crows still scolded that exact mask.
slides.image_prompt: Black crow perched on a branch staring directly forward, sharp eye in focus, soft morning light, dark green background

slides.title: They pass on the grudge
slides.body: Crows that were never trapped learned to scold the mask too, by copying the others.
slides.image_prompt: Group of black crows on a power line, several turned toward the same point, overcast sky

slides.title: They judge the face
slides.body: A neutral mask worn on the same walks got almost no scolding. Only the 'dangerous' face mattered.
slides.image_prompt: Two plain masks hanging on a tree branch, one dark and one pale, a crow perched nearby watching them

slides.title: Brain scans agree
slides.body: Seeing the threatening face lit up crow brain areas linked to fear and learning, much like ours.
slides.image_prompt: Glowing stylised bird brain floating above a crow silhouette, warm orange light inside, dark blue background

caption:
In 2006, researchers at the University of Washington wore a caveman mask while trapping a few wild crows. Years later, crows on campus still dive-bombed and scolded anyone wearing that mask, even birds that were never caught.

Crows learn faces, share warnings with each other and remember for years. Tomorrow's Part 2 covers what else these birds can do. Follow so you don't miss it.

Have you ever had a bird that seemed to recognise you?
